author: reek
body: `usb-kbd-connect` drives `kbd-connect`, which walks the ROOT ports and nothing else. That is not the code the boot payload runs: `GopBoot` calls `usb-attach`, and `usb-attach` walks hubs. So the hub walk -- `usb-open-hub`, `hub-walk`, `hub-attach-port`, and the transaction translator arithmetic in them -- had never been executed by anything, on any emulator, in any battery. It is the code that runs on the machine the campaign exists for, and it was the code nobody could see.

author: reek
body: codex-vm presents a high-speed hub on root port 4 with a FULL-SPEED boot keyboard on its one downstream port. That is the topology the hypothesis is about: a full-speed device below a high-speed hub reaches the bus only through that hub's transaction translator, and the controller learns which one from the TT Hub Slot ID and TT Port Number in the slot context. The model refuses to service a periodic endpoint whose slot names no translator, exactly as silicon does -- so a driver that leaves those fields zero enumerates perfectly and then hears nothing, which is the reported shape of the failure on the ASUS.

author: reek
body: The root keyboard is unplugged for this test (`-xhci-no-root-kbd`), because the walk takes the first keyboard it finds and root port 2 comes first. Same guest binary, different bus.

author: reek
body: `usb-kbd-hub2` is the same question one tier deeper, where the hub the keyboard is plugged into is not the hub that translates for it.

author: reek
body: What each line proves. `route` non-zero says the keyboard was reached THROUGH the hub rather than off a root port -- without it every line below would be the root-attached case wearing this test's name. `speed=1` says it is full speed, so a translator is genuinely required. `code` is the completion, and it is the whole question: it can only be non-negative if the slot context named a transaction translator, because the controller declines to schedule the endpoint otherwise.
